source.title: The Status of Polycyclic Group-Based Cryptography: A Survey and Open Problems

accepted.question_text: For polycyclic groups given by polycyclic presentations, determine a global computational complexity analysis for the collection algorithm used to solve the word problem. In particular, can the complexity be bounded in terms of the input word, rather than depending on the absolute values of exponents that arise during the intermediate collection process?

evidence.quote: The collection algorithm is generally effective in practical applications, but its precise computational complexity remains unknown.
The resultant worst-case bound is in terms of the absolute values of all exponents occurring during the collection process, rather than the exponents of the input word.
Thus a global complexity analysis of the collection algorithm remains elusive.

accepted.question_text: For the collection approach to polycyclic groups that finds a large nilpotent normal subgroup and then uses the Malcev correspondence for that subgroup, determine the computational complexity of this Malcev-structure-based methodology.

evidence.quote: This approach determines a large nilpotent normal subgroup of the given group and then exploits the Malcev correspondence for the normal subgroup.
There is no known complexity analysis for this methodology.

accepted.question_text: For infinite polycyclic groups of high Hirsch length, determine whether there are algorithms that solve the conjugacy search problem effectively, and give computational complexity bounds for such algorithms if they exist. The question concerns the high-Hirsch-length regime where existing methods for the conjugacy search problem are not known to apply efficiently.
accepted.context_brief: conjugacy search at high Hirsch length

evidence.quote: The algorithm has been implemented and seems to be efficient for groups of small Hirsch length.
Presently there are no known algorithms for infinite polycyclic groups of high Hirsch length.

accepted.question_text: Given two polycyclic groups by finite presentations, with the promise that they are isomorphic, determine the computational complexity of the isomorphism search problem: finding an explicit isomorphism between the two groups, rather than merely deciding whether an isomorphism exists.

evidence.quote: Isomorphism Decision Problem - Given groups G and G′ with respective finite presentations hX | Ri and hX ′ | R′ i, determine if G is isomorphic to G′ .
Once the solvability of a group-theoretic decision problem is affirmed, the subsequent task is to produce elements (or morphisms, etc.) that are solutions to particular instances of it.
(1) What is the complexity of the isomorphism search problem in polycyclic groups?

accepted.question_text: Let G be a polycyclic group and let phi be an endomorphism of G. Given elements w and t in G with the promise that at least one element a in G satisfies t = a^-1 w phi(a), determine the computational complexity of finding such an element a. Equivalently, determine the complexity of the twisted conjugacy search problem in polycyclic groups.

evidence.quote: The twisted conjugacy search problems is to find, given a group G and an endomorphism φ, an element a ∈ G such that t = a−1 wφ(a), provided that at least one such a exists.
(2) What is the complexity of the twisted search conjugacy problem in poly- cyclic groups?

accepted.question_text: Let G be a polycyclic group. Given elements a and b in G, with the promise that there exist an integer n in N and an element g in G such that a^n = b^g, determine the computational complexity of finding such an exponent n and conjugating element g. This is the power conjugacy search problem in polycyclic groups.

evidence.quote: The key exchange presented in Section 3.3.2 makes use of the power conjugacy search problem, where if it is known for some a, b ∈ G and n ∈ N that an = bg for some g ∈ G, the task is to find one such n and g.
(3) What is the complexity of the power conjugacy problem in polycyclic groups?

accepted.question_text: Every polycyclic group can be embedded into GL(n, Z) for some natural number n, and matrix representations can be computed in some special cases such as torsion-free nilpotent groups. Determine the computational complexity of finding a matrix representation of a polycyclic group.

evidence.quote: It is well-known that every polycyclic group can be embed- ded into GL(n, Z) for some n ∈ N.
For groups that are additionally torsion-free and nilpotent, a matrix representation can be computed.
(6) What is the complexity of finding matrix representation of polycyclic groups?

accepted.question_text: Let G be a polycyclic group and let Aut(G) be its automorphism group. Given automorphisms of G, determine the computational complexity of the conjugacy problem in Aut(G), that is, the problem of deciding whether the automorphisms are conjugate inside the automorphism group.

evidence.quote: For groups G in the larger class of polycyclic-by-finite (or virtually polycyclic) groups, the conjugacy decision problem is decidable in Aut(G) [38].
(7) What is the complexity of the conjugacy problem in the automorphism of polycyclic groups?

accepted.question_text: For polycyclic groups, determine the computational complexity of the search endomorphism problem and its automorphism variant. In the endomorphism version supported by the source text, the input includes a group S and elements s and t with the promise that t = phi(s) for some endomorphism phi from S to S, and the task is to find such an endomorphism; the automorphism variant asks the analogous question when the map is required to be an automorphism.

evidence.quote: The endomorphism search problem in S should be demonstrably NP-hard.
Alice chooses an endomorphism φ : S → S as her private key. Alice then chooses elements s, t ∈ S such that t = φ(s).
(8) What is the complexity of the search endomorphism (automorphism) prob- lem in polycyclic groups?

accepted.question_text: Determine whether cryptosystems based on polycyclic groups, especially those using infinite polycyclic groups, are resistant to cryptanalysis by quantum algorithms. Equivalently, establish whether such polycyclic group-based cryptosystems remain secure against quantum computers, in light of the source text's observation that known quantum algorithms discussed there apply to finite-group settings rather than infinite groups.

evidence.quote: Of particular interest is to show that cryptosystems using infinite polycyclic groups are resistant to cryptanalysis on a quantum com- puter.
Despite these developments in the use quantum algorithms for finite groups, there are no known quantum algorithms that are applicable to infinite groups.
(10) Are polycyclic group-based cryptosystems resistant to quantum algorithms?

accepted.question_text: For general polycyclic groups used as platform groups in group-based cryptography, determine bounds on the dimensions of the smallest faithful linear embeddings and determine when faithful linear representations are known and small enough for linear decomposition or linear centralizer attacks to be tractable.

evidence.quote: Moreover, the linear space into which the group is embedded must be of sufficiently small dimension to make the attack tractable.
no such bounds are known for other linear groups, including general polycyclic groups and metabelian groups.
The applicability of the linear centralizer attack to other platform groups is limited to those whose faithful representations are known and whose linear repre- sentations are sufficiently small.
these aspects of polycyclic groups are currently unknown.

trace.notes: Normalized the original zbMATH URL as a bibliographic resolver. Local index metadata identified the same work as DOI 10.1515/gcc-2016-0013 with arXiv link 1607.05819; the cached arXiv PDF was used as the readable primary artifact because shell DNS access to zbmath.org and api.zbmath.org failed in this sandbox.

Mapped the PDF table of contents and section structure: Section 2 covers algorithmic problems in polycyclic groups, Section 3 covers cryptosystems, Section 4 covers cryptanalysis and attacks, and Section 5 contains the numbered open-problem list.
Extracted implicit complexity questions for the collection algorithm and the Malcev-based collection methodology from the representations subsection.
Extracted conjugacy-search variants, including the high-Hirsch-length algorithm gap, power conjugacy search, and twisted conjugacy search.
Extracted the endomorphism search setting from the authentication-scheme section because the conclusion asks for the complexity of search endomorphism and automorphism problems.
Extracted the unresolved linear-embedding-size issue affecting linear decomposition and linear centralizer attacks.
Extracted all eleven explicit numbered outstanding problems in the conclusion.
Expanded the implicit collection-algorithm complexity gap using the page 4 discussion of intermediate exponents and missing global bounds.
Rewrote the Malcev-methodology gap as a standalone complexity-analysis question using the local description of the method.
Rewrote the high-Hirsch-length algorithm gap for the conjugacy search problem without adding a model beyond the source text.
Expanded the isomorphism search problem using the source's decision-problem definition and its statement that search variants produce morphisms or other witnesses.
Expanded the conclusion's twisted-search shorthand using the source's definition of twisted conjugacy search.
Expanded the conclusion's power-conjugacy shorthand using the source's definition of power conjugacy search.
The source lists the geodesic length problem but does not define it in the readable artifact, so the item was kept for review.
The source lists the n-root problem but does not define it in the readable artifact, so the item was kept for review.
Inlined the paper's statement that polycyclic groups embed into GL(n, Z) and that matrix representations are computable in special cases.
Used the source's Aut(G) decidability statement to restate the open complexity question for conjugacy in automorphism groups.
Expanded the endomorphism-search question using the authentication-scheme setup where phi is private and t = phi(s) is public evidence.
The conclusion lists the homomorphism problem but the source text does not give enough local definition to make a self-contained rewrite.
Combined the abstract's infinite-polycyclic quantum-resistance objective with Section 2.6 and the conclusion's quantum-algorithm open problem.
The source defines subgroup membership as a decision problem but does not provide enough local definition of the search variant to make a no-new-facts rewrite.
Rewrote the unresolved linear-embedding-size issue as a cryptanalysis-relevant question about faithful representations of general polycyclic groups.

Kept matrix-representation complexity and smallest-linear-embedding bounds as separate questions because the former asks about finding a representation and the latter asks about dimensional bounds relevant to attacks.
Accepted items have page-located evidence and self-contained rewrites. Items with undefined or insufficiently defined source-specific search-problem terminology were moved to needs_review.
